7.5a — Design a Big Cave: Flow & Difficulty

You have all the tools — tiles, enemies, ladders, spikes, turrets. Tools do not make a level; flow does. Today, zero code: you learn to read a level like a designer, sketch your whole big cave on paper, and only then paint it.

Concept Lab ~20 min

1. Flow: the path is the message. Players move toward: open space, light, coins, and AWAY from spikes and enemies. A level steers without a single word.

Good: room → glimpse of next room through a gap → curiosity pulls
Bad:  room → identical exits left/right both dark → player stops,
      and a stopped player reads the room as a wall

2. Pacing: the beat chart. Any good cave is a rhythm of TENSION (threat) and RELEASE (safety + reward):

SectionBeatFeel
1 Entrancequiet"I belong here"
2 Teethtensionspike jumps — first death possible
3 Ladder + turretrelease → tensionclimb while shot at
4 Rest + coinsreleasebreath, spend coins mentally
5 Gauntletpeak tensioneverything at once
6 Boss doorquietthe door says "next time"

3. Difficulty curve (again, at scale). The personality-turret ramp from 3.4a was three copies of a knob; this is the same idea with rooms. Rule of thumb: each section may introduce ONE new combination (spikes + turret = one new thing; not spikes + turret + ladder + moving platform = four).

4. Signposting: telegraph everything. Safe routes look safe. Danger is visible BEFORE it is threatening (the turret is seen at rest before it shoots). The exit is visible from the entrance (or glimpsed once). Your soft gate from 6.4a is signposting for the boots.

Socratic

Difficulty and fairness are different axes: hard-but-fair vs easy-but-random. Using sightlines and telegraphs, explain how your cave can be the FIRST while your random-placement impulse (we all have it) makes the SECOND. Which one do testers call "good" even when they die?

Design Lab ~25 min

Step 1 — the paper sketch. Pencil, one page, your whole cave: all 6 beats as rooms/boxes, with arrows for the path and notes for threats. No detail on any single screen — flow first. This paper IS the design; the tilemap is just a transcription of it.

Step 2 — the camera question. Your game camera shows a fixed width. Mark on your sketch what is VISIBLE at each beat: what does the player see from section 2? They should see the goal of section 2 and the PROMISE of section 3 (a glimpse, a light, a coin trail). Adjust boxes so each screen shows: this beat's challenge + a hint of the next one.

Step 3 — the death audit. Walk your sketch and ask at every beat: if the player dies HERE, what do they lose? Under 20 seconds of progress = healthy. Over 60 = spite (either add a checkpoint trigger, or shorten the section — your 2.2a respawn loop is all you get unless you build checkpoints, which you may).

Bug Hunt: Design smell test

  1. Sketch audit: is there ANY beat that introduces two new things at once? Which thing moves to a later beat?
  2. Stand (mentally) in beat 4 (rest) — can the player see a spike from there? Why must rest beats be visually clean of threats?
  3. Count screens between the boss door and the last save/heal. Is your potion before or after the peak tension — and why do great games heal BEFORE the boss, not after?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Trade sketches

  1. Trade sketches with a partner. They point at any box: you must say the BEAT and the FEEL sentence in five seconds. If you hesitate, the sketch is not clear enough yet.
  2. Partner marks your path with a pencil "blind" — where do THEY think the player will go? Anywhere their line diverges from your intended path is a signposting bug found for free.
  3. Commit + push a photo/scan of the final sketch: "7.5a: cave sketch + beat chart". The sketch goes in the repo — design docs are code.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain flow, pacing, difficulty curve, signposting — each in one sentence
  • Draw a 6-beat cave sketch with path arrows and threat notes
  • Run a camera-visibility pass and a death audit on your sketch
  • Explain hard-but-fair vs easy-but-random with examples from your own sketch
